rationale: This is a genuine internal-consistency fix rather than a cosmetic tweak — the archive's best-slope signal adds R&D to the numerator while leaving the capital base understated, and capitalizing a five-year R&D stock in the denominator is the coherent completion of that adjustment, with a specific and testable diagnosis (long-leg contamination) for why slope improved without alpha improving.

Changing the accrual deflator from total assets to non-cash current assets is a marginal scaling variant of an already-tested hurdle, and the deflator is internally mismatched with the numerator (a net working-capital accrual divided by a gross current-asset base), which also invites instability and outlier-driven ranks in firms with thin working capital.

The Sloan-style total-accrual definition is a legitimate and cleanly motivated accrual-definition test inside the hurdle structure, but the claim that this dimension has never been varied is inaccurate — the same depreciation-inclusive accrual was used in AccrualGradedProfitability and the depreciation channel in DepreciationBackedProfit, both of which produced strong slopes with negligible alpha, so prior evidence already hints this variant will dilute portfolio evidence.

A second-moment hurdle is a substantively different construct and worth one test, but the archive's prior implementation of this exact channel produced an insignificant slope (1.49) alongside significantly negative alpha, and since MIN rewards high stability just as the product did, the failure is more likely directional than structural — the "recast as a hurdle fixes it" argument is asserted rather than evidenced.

This is a mechanical recombination of two already-evaluated legs (the R&D-adjusted profitability numerator and the own-history working-capital-days hurdle, each tested at gen 5–6) with no new economic content beyond "pair the two best components," so its outcome is largely predictable from the existing archive.

A tail/max-based accrual hurdle is genuinely distinct from the level, three-year mean, five-year sum, sign-frequency, and volatility variants, the asymmetry argument (punish spikes, still reward releases) is economically coherent and correctly matched to the expression's sign, and it poses a sharp discriminating test against the volatility hurdle — though its likely high correlation with the existing three-year-mean hurdle caps the expected incremental information.
